# Summary of the 1997 Liberal Democrats Manifesto

## Core Vision
The Liberal Democrats' 1997 manifesto, titled "Make the Difference," presented a programme centred on building a fair, free, and open society. The party positioned itself as rejecting political timidity, promising active government that invests in people while balancing liberty, equality, and community values.

## Education: The Top Priority
Education formed the manifesto's cornerstone commitment. The party pledged an additional £2 billion annually for education, funded by raising income tax by 1p in the pound. Key priorities included providing early years education for all 3-4 year olds, doubling spending on school books and equipment, reducing primary class sizes to maximum 30 pupils within five years, and tackling building repairs. The manifesto also promoted lifelong learning through Individual Learning Accounts and opposed university top-up fees.

## Economic Policy
The party advocated for economic stability through an independent Bank of England, supported joining a single European currency (subject to meeting criteria and a referendum), and promoted enterprise through support for small businesses. They proposed shifting taxation from employment towards pollution and resource depletion as part of their environmental strategy.

## Environmental Commitments
Environmental protection featured prominently, with proposals to cut carbon dioxide emissions by 30% over 15 years, introduce a carbon tax on fossil fuels (offset by cuts to VAT and National Insurance), launch a National Homes Insulation programme, and invest in public transport while trebling rail freight capacity.

## Health and Social Policy
For the NHS, the party promised £540 million extra annually, 10,000 more nurses or 5,000 more doctors, maximum six-month waiting times, and restored free eye and dental checks. On welfare, they proposed helping the long-term unemployed through a Benefit Transfer Programme and breaking poverty traps by raising tax thresholds.

## Constitutional Reform
The manifesto outlined ambitious democratic reforms: proportional representation for all elections, a Bill of Rights incorporating the European Convention on Human Rights, Freedom of Information legislation, House of Lords reform, Scottish and Welsh devolution with tax-raising powers, and stronger local government.

## Conclusion
The manifesto concluded by acknowledging that quality services require investment, explicitly rejecting the possibility of simultaneous tax cuts, and asking voters to make that choice.
